Your Project Name: Beyond Surfaces: The Many Faces of Layer
Your Project Description (max 2000 chara:
This body of work investigates the concept of “Layer” as both a visual
strategy and a methodological framework. Beginning with a translation
of Photoshop’s digital layer logic into a physical system using tracing
paper, the experiments first explored how rules, variables, and chance
operations can generate layered outcomes. Building on this, the project
then extended into natural analogies by simulating mineral banding
through watercolor, where time and angle were introduced as variables
to mimic geological processes of accumulation and crystallization.
Across these iterations, “Layer” is examined not only as a design
technique, but also as a language of growth, memory, and transformation.
By shifting from digital to physical and then to natural systems, the work
demonstrates the multiple possibilities of layering—revealing how layers
can structure visual complexity, embody temporal processes, and record
hidden forces shaping both design and nature.
File 1 description: This body of work investigates the concept of “Layer” as both a visual strategy and a methodological framework. Beginning with a translation of Photoshop’s digital layer logic into a physical system using tracing paper, the experiments first explored how rules, variables, and chance operations can generate layered outcomes.
File 2 description: Through overlapping transparency, new hues and intricate intersections emerged. The resulting compositions were documented and reassembled into graphic posters, translating a digital concept of layering into a tactile, generative process.
File 3 description: Building on the previous tracing paper layering study, this iteration explores the metaphor of mineral crystal growth. Using watercolor and controlled physical conditions, each layer is created by timed pigment pulses on a wetted surface. Two key variables — time intervals and board tilt angles — are introduced to influence how colors expand and settle. The process documents how abstract geological growth can be translated into a visual system, generating organic, ring-like formations that echo natural strata.

Your Project Description (max 2000 chara:
The "Entropy Clock" is an interdisciplinary project exploring the perception of time. It eschews the abstract timekeeping of clocks and returns to a primal experience grounded in the transformations of matter.
The project draws inspiration from the concept of "entropy" — the irreversible process by which the universe shifts from order to disorder. This irreversible increase in entropy is precisely our most intuitive perception of time.
Therefore, the "Entropy Clock" eschews the scales of seconds, minutes, and hours, instead defining the passage of time by measuring the changes in the state of things themselves.
We embody this concept through two experiments:
Incense Ash Score: The burning of incense is conceived as a "concert of time," its fading into ash becoming a clock cycle, and the ash traces becoming a visual
"score" of time.
Timing by Ice Melting: Time is perceived by observing the melting of ice into water. The disappearance of form reflects the increasing entropy and the irreversible nature of time.
The "Entropy Clock" transforms time from a digital form into a tangible experience, inviting people to pay attention to the rhythms of things themselves and reconsider their essential connection to time.
File 1 description: The burning of incense is considered a "concert of time." The process of the incense's decay from order to disorder (dissolving into smoke and ash) becomes a clock cycle, and the resulting ash trail becomes a visual "musical score" of time.
File 2 description: I recorded the smoke and ash from burning incense sticks, and put them together to make a piece of incense ash music score.
File 3 description: This piece of ice perceives time by observing the process of ice melting from a solid state into water. The gradual blurring and disappearance of the ice's physical boundaries clearly reflects the physical nature of increasing entropy and the irreversibility of time.

Your Project Description (max 2000 chara:
A library is traditionally a highly ordered space, where books are strictly 
classified and catalogued. The Chance Archive seeks to disrupt this logic. In each 
experiment, I begin by determining a starting point, then draw Move, Choose, 
and Act instruction cards to navigate the real space until I am randomly led to a 
book, whose 100th page I record. That book’s position becomes the destination. 
Afterwards, I enter this start–end pair into p5.js, with another rule: rolling dice, 
changing direction every ten steps, until one hundred steps are completed. The 
program generates a simulated path accordingly.
Both trajectories—bodily action and computational generation—are preserved as 
“chance encounters.” As these paths and pages accumulate, they form The Chance 
Archive, revealing that knowledge acquisition need not follow catalogic order 
but can also be sparked by chance, turning reading into a game of exploration and 
discovery.
File 1 description:
This project consists of two interrelated “routes.”
First, by randomly drawing index cards, I followed their instructions to reach a specific book in the library, creating a physical path driven by chance.
Then, I input the starting and ending points of this path into p5.js, which generated a 100-step random route based on the rule of rolling dice every ten steps to decide the direction.
The 100th page of the corresponding book was scanned and archived according to my self-created index card sequence. By juxtaposing the chance-based physical trajectory with the algorithmically generated path, the project establishes a connection between chance, knowledge, and image. Through the combination of algorithmic diagrams and book archives, it presents a research and creative approach grounded in randomness.

Your Project Description (max 2000 chara: In this experiment, we chose paper as the core material and dripped cola onto notebook paper, kitchen paper, watercolor paper, and napkins. By observing the diffusion speed, edge clarity, and distribution of high-moisture areas over 5 to 30 seconds, we documented each material’s unique behavior. Your Project Description (max 2000 chara:
This work is a system that transforms errors occurring in the process of machine
text recognition into new visual and physical outcomes. By scanning diverse
sources—such as clothing labels, packaging, books, and handwriting—the
project experiments with how accurately machines can recognize text depending
on resolution and typeface. The detected errors are extracted and converted
into circular dot patterns, which expand beyond the digital screen into physical
artifacts through laser cutting.

In particular, recognized text areas are translated into line-based circular structures
rather than filled forms, revealing a fragmented stratum of language that seems
both readable and unreadable. Viewers encounter familiar words disassembled
and recomposed into visual structures, simultaneously experiencing the instability
of language and the limitations of machine recognition.

Rather than framing errors as “failures,” this system reinterprets them as a new
visual language. In doing so, it transforms unreadability itself into a resource,
prompting reflection on the relationship between humans and machines, and on
the shifting boundary between reading and seeing.

My project is surrounding my quote: Passion fuels purpose. It's a very simple quote but something that I reflect on everyday. Design wise when I started this molecule. I wanted to do something that wasn't too simple, maybe something a little 3D to make up for the short quote. 

So I made 8 quadrilaterals. All custom shapes. The first four were the big ones. Then I did the smaller ones. I would say that positioning these shapes off center was the most challenging. Of course, I could center them but I wanted to keep my quote off centered to bring more dynamic to the composition. 

After I finished the shapes, we were learning about GUI & randomization. To add these components into my work I did randomization for canvas size. I picked my minimum and maximum size so it would vary from those options. I added a GUI to change size as well if I wanted to manually change it if I didn't want that run of code. Previously before my last change of my code, all of it was based on the one run of code. Unless you press the run again. No loop for my code. My last GUI I added was the stroke thickness. 

The following week I added the "if, else" variables to my code. With these I did color change. Of course I had my regular colors picked but to make it dynamic I chose when the randomization picked a canvas size, it would correspond with a darker or lighter color of the original option. If the canvas size was bigger it would be darker. If the canvas size was small, it would be lighter. 

My last thing I added was the loop for changing font. I took feedback from my classmates when presenting. And learned that I could have made my 5 variations of my code stronger if I chose different fonts displayed in the prints. So I took it upon myself to do a last minute edit to have this in mind. I coded a frame rate of 1, but each time it is a new frame, it is a new canvas size, a new color and a new font.

Your Project Description (max 2000 chara: I chose this quote because of my love for ice cream -- making it, enjoying it and being drawn to its playful colours. The manifesto uses ice cream as a metaphor for life's fleeting moments, encouraging us to savour joy before it melts away. Through colour, melting letterforms, capturing vibrancy and impermanence of life. Transforming something simple and sweet into a declaration to live fully.
File 1 description:
I began my coding process on P5 by focusing on the concept: I wanted to turn my manifesto quote “life is like an ice cream, enjoy it before it melts” into a playful, visual system. Ice cream is colourful, temporary, and fun—so I wanted my code to reflect that same feeling through sprinkles, a cone, and a scoop that carries the text.I started with a configuration section where I defined the key variables: the quote, background color, font, sprinkle count, and two “flavor” variations (strawberry and mint). This allowed me to control the whole design with a few parameters instead of rewriting code later.I generated a pastel backdrop filled with sprinkles. Using randomness for position, size, angle, and color gave the background an organic, scattered feel—similar to how real sprinkles fall onto ice cream.
I built the cone using many horizontal lines that gradually shift color, giving a shaded, gradient look. To emphasize the waffle texture, I added crosshatch lines. This step was about making the base of the ice cream visually believable while still stylized.
The scoop rim was designed with overlapping translucent ellipses and “bumps,” which made the edge look fluffy and irregular, like melting ice cream. This added depth and softness to balance the hard geometry of the cone.
The most important part was wrapping the manifesto text around the scoop. I split the sentence into individual characters, calculated their circular positions, and rotated each one upright. This made the text feel like it was part of the scoop itself rather than just sitting on top.To bring the design alive, I programmed:
Drips: characters on the bottom arc occasionally drip, simulating melting. I tied this to frameCount so it changes over time.
Gloss and sparkle: each letter was given a highlight ellipse and a rare random sparkle, imitating the shiny, sticky surface of ice cream.
These dynamic effects emphasized the manifesto’s idea of impermanence.

Your Project Name: “The water passes over the stone, but still moves forward.“
Your Project Description (max 2000 chara:
“The water passes over the stone, but still moves forward. “This sentence is the base of my work. It shows meaning in both concept and code.
In my sketch, stones are the problem. Water is man. The white and blue lines move across the screen. They show different ways in which people deal with obstacles. People, like water, do not use a fixed way. They tried many methods. They change the intensity and direction to solve the difficulty. When water hits a stone, it bends. Problems leave their mark. It makes people think. It provides new ideas. It may even change them. In my code, this is shown as a repeated curve. Each line together forms a rhythm. This rhythm is like a memory being repeated in the mind. When the water is constantly flowing, the adaptation becomes apparent. The white lines represent past problems that have been solved. Once people have encountered the same problem many times, they know what to do. The blue line shows the new strength. People acquire skills by doing. They are prepared for future problems. When the mouse is placed on the stone, as if the dilemma is mentioned again, the swing amplitude of the water flow becomes larger, which represents people's exclamation and reflection on the dilemma.
When I write code, I often think about how to use simple shapes and colors to show my ideas. I don't want to complicate the picture too much. The process is step by step. I'm going to write a part of it, and then I'll see how it works. Sometimes it didn't look right, so I changed the size, the speed, or the color. I kept testing until it felt clear. This process helped me understand how simple tools can create many different outcomes. Shapes and colors may seem basic, but they can tell different stories.

Your Project Description (max 2000 chara:
This project—through a poster, visual map, coded work, and installation—explores the journey of letting go. I built the narrative around the quote: “If you surrender to the air, you can ride it.” My research focused on the tension between ego and higher self, and how surrender requires both reflection and faith. The heart becomes central in this act, representing belief and trust, while the brain resists, creating an internal battle between control and release.

Digitally, I used code to translate these ideas into action and instance—particles scattering and reforming, waves shifting in layered perspective, and interactive images responding to the viewer’s presence. These choices became metaphors for chaos, resistance, and eventual calm, using motion and interaction to visualize the act of surrender.

The visual map blended imagery of a brain and heart, symbolizing how intellect and emotion must work together for true submission. Artifacts such as handcuffs, a puppet master, and a contemplative figure looking toward the sky highlight moments of restraint, control, and release.

In the installation, mirrors served as both surface and metaphor. As viewers looked down into their reflection, their posture naturally shifted into a position of surrender—head lowered, back turned to the projection behind them. This blocking of the projection emphasized that true surrender is not external but internal.

Across mediums, the work reflects surrender as a layered process: chaotic, reflective, and ultimately freeing.

Supporting artifacts anchor this narrative in personal history. They include archival photos of my mother from her younger years to evoke a sense of nostalgia and the desire to uncover her stories, and a symbolic envelope to represent the theme of the unanswered letter.

Your Project Description (max 2000 chara:
This project is based on El Jacho, a Puerto Rican folklore tale most closely tied to the coastal town of Salinas. The story follows a fisherman who, one stormy night, lost the light of his lantern while out at sea. In desperation, he set fire to the wooden cross he carried for protection, hoping it would guide him back to shore. This act of burning a sacred object brought a curse upon him. In some versions, the fisherman sickened and died soon after. In others, he never died at all but became a restless figure, doomed to wander the coast forever in search of the ashes of the cross he destroyed. People say that on certain nights a flickering light can be seen drifting along the shore, the ghostly presence of El Jacho.

For my design response, I selected three artefacts that capture the story’s cycle of cause, action, and consequence. The lantern represents the fisherman’s failing source of light and the initial event that set the story in motion. The flame or match symbolizes the desperate act of burning the cross, an irreversible choice. The rope knot embodies the eternal binding of the curse and serves as a metaphor for being trapped in an endless fate.

To analyze the narrative, I created a Lynch-style map that presents the two main characters, the fisherman and the entity that curses him, and traces the decisions that led to his fate.

The first iteration of the installation was staged in a corner space as an experiment in material and atmosphere. Draped fabrics were used to test the amount needed to suggest the sea and surrounding environment. Corded string was arranged to represent scattered ashes or the burning embers of the cross. This prototype served as a base to explore how the story can be translated into space, and future versions will build on it with the introduction of the lantern, flame, and knot along with additional materials and interactions.
